strengths: Elegant theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.1 establishes a meaningful discrete analog of the Benamou-Brenier theorem, deriving Kantorovich formulations for discrete flows with clear connections to transport costs and similarity metrics

Well-motivated problem formulation: Identifies genuine limitations in discrete flow matching (inability to rectify, lack of density estimation) and proposes principled solutions grounded in optimal transport theory
Rigorous mathematical development: Proofs are carefully constructed with proper handling of technical details (e.g., O(ε²) terms in Theorem 4.1), demonstrating competent mathematical execution
Practical insights: Shows how similarity metric choices map to cost functions and connects token embeddings to OT formulations, providing actionable guidance for practitioners
Clear exposition of foundations: Sections 2.1-2.3 provide systematic and accessible treatment of discrete-time/continuous-time Markov chains and discrete flow matching
weaknesses: Critical: Completely absent experimental validation. No experiments comparing proposed minibatch OT to baselines, validating perplexity bound utility, or demonstrating practical improvements. This is disqualifying for ICML even for theoretical papers, as it leaves the practical applicability entirely unassessed

Moderate theoretical novelty: Theorem 3.1 primarily applies existing OT theory to specific flow structures (Eqs. 7-9); minibatch OT is largely an application of Tong et al. (2023); Theorem 4.1 closely builds on Opper & Sanguinetti (2007) and Lou et al. (2024)

Perplexity bound practical utility unclear: No analysis of bound tightness or informativeness; Eq. (24) requires computing expectations over trajectories with unspecified computational complexity; no experiments demonstrating when the bound is useful versus vacuous

Limited scope: Results apply only to convex interpolant flows; generalization to other designs unaddressed. Dynamic evolution of embeddings during training (Corollary 3.3) is not rigorously analyzed despite its importance

Training stability inadequately addressed: Discussion of embedding decoupling is brief with no convergence analysis; claim that 'local view stabilizes' training lacks rigorous justification; joint optimization of coupling and flow lacks theoretical analysis

Source distribution selection unmotivated: Two heuristics proposed (empirical frequency, K-means) without principled justification or empirical comparison; missing analysis of transportation cost reduction achievable with different choices

Incomplete contributions: Chain-of-flows (Section 5) deferred to future work but contributes nothing; computational complexity of minibatch OT and bound computation not discussed; scalability properties unknown

Presentation gaps: Transition from Eq. (17) to (18) lacks clear motivation; Benamou-Brenier connection mentioned but underdeveloped; definition of p̄ₜ scattered across multiple equations; limited engagement with broader OT literature
Reproducibility concerns: No code provided, no experiments to reproduce, sparse implementation details; computing Eq. (24) would require substantial non-trivial implementation effort

Section 5 on chains of flows relegated to 'future work' with no theoretical analysis, convergence guarantees, or guidance on when beneficial
Limited intuition provided for theoretical results; dense mathematical exposition without clear explanation of practical implications

Rigorous mathematical contributions: Theorem 3.1 elegantly derives Kantorovich equivalence for arbitrary similarity metrics, with insightful corollaries recovering Hamming and L2 norms
Theorem 4.1 properly bounds KL divergence and enables computable perplexity upper bound for discrete flows
Clear presentation with detailed proofs and good intuition for design choices (e.g., embedding-based similarity metric)
Discusses practical considerations (training stability, source distribution strategies) showing awareness of implementation challenges

Section 5 on Chains of Flows is speculative future work rather than concrete contribution, with authors acknowledging uncertainty
Perplexity bound computation (Eq. 24) involves expensive summation over discrete states; no guidance on practical estimation or when bound becomes vacuous

strengths: Sound theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.1 establishing equivalence between weighted path-length dynamic formulation and Kantorovich dual is well-motivated, rigorously proven, and naturally accommodates general similarity measures beyond L2

Principled perplexity bounds with strong empirical validation: two complementary bounds (Theorems 4.1-4.2) derived for DFM, with 0.96 Pearson correlation between bounds and generative perplexity confirming practical utility

Comprehensive experimental methodology: thorough computational overhead analysis (3.4% at batch 512 with favorable scaling), multiple evaluation metrics (different judges, entropy preservation, standard deviations), and extensive ablations demonstrating robustness
Careful bound tightness analysis: empirical validation in simplified settings showing ~11% gap comparable to continuous diffusion theory, supporting validity of approximations
Novel categorical Benamou-Brenier-type theorem: extends OT theory to discrete settings with similarity-based costs, providing new theoretical tools for discrete generative modeling
weaknesses: Restricted theorem applicability: Theorem 3.1 applies only to convex interpolants with specific form (Eq. 4); generalization to non-convex interpolants and other flow types unclear, limiting theoretical scope

Improvements limited to artificial BoW sources: headline 8× step reduction only applies to bag-of-words distributions which are not standard practice; evaluation on realistic source distributions (uniform masking, real data) absent
Substantial performance gap persists: DFM-MMLM-OT achieves ~143.5 perplexity vs. GPT2's 58.92 on realistic benchmarks (Table 2), limiting practical significance despite theoretical advances

Perplexity bound limitations underemphasized: bounds depend on unknown probability ratios (Appendix A.5) making them intractable for exact computation; ~11% empirical gap and unknown tightness at scale not highlighted sufficiently in main text

Multimask flow contribution appears ad-hoc: lacks rigorous justification for why OT cannot apply to standard masked flows; solution of doubling vocabulary with 50K special tokens feels engineered rather than principled; modest ~5-10% improvements

Unresolved two-loop optimization analysis: minibatch OT and flow training form coupled loops where embedding updates change optimal coupling; Section 7 dismisses concerns based on claimed 'stability' without theoretical or empirical justification of convergence

Limited comparison to concurrent work: Shaul et al. (2025) kinetic-energy formulation mentioned but not thoroughly compared; insufficient discussion of how contributions differentiate from related work

strengths: Theoretically sound: Theorem 3.1 correctly establishes equivalence between dynamic and Kantorovich formulations for discrete flows with convex interpolants; proofs appear rigorous.
Principled perplexity bounds: Extending bounds from discrete diffusion to DFM addresses a genuine problem; enables model comparison and provides training objectives.
Comprehensive empirical validation: Includes toy experiments validating theory, bound tightness analysis on small problems, and realistic scale experiments on OWT.
Practical implementation details: Computational overhead analysis (~3.4%) demonstrates feasibility; clear algorithms provided for reproducibility.
Well-written mathematical exposition: The preliminaries and theoretical sections are generally clear and accessible.
weaknesses: Incremental theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.1 adapts the Benamou-Brenier theorem to per-position flows—a restricted case. Minibatch OT applies existing methods (Tong et al. 2024). Perplexity bounds closely follow Haxholli et al. (2025); concurrent work (Shaul et al. 2025) independently obtained similar results.

Misleading empirical claims: The '8-fold reduction' (1024→128 steps) is technically true but represents only 0.03% perplexity difference (185.12→185.06). Framing as achieving 'same generative perplexity' at 8× fewer steps is misleading when the improvement is negligible.

Weak experimental improvements: Comparison with SEDD shows no clear wins (DFM-N: 53.19 vs SEDD: 52.18 on Lambada). DFM consistently trails GPT-2 significantly (49.02 vs 77.87), suggesting fundamental limitations rather than optimization issues.

Loose perplexity bounds: ~11% gap between bounds and ground truth in toy experiments; bounds depend on intractable probability ratios between neighbor states, limiting practical utility. No analysis of tightness scaling with vocabulary or sequence length.

Multimask flows feel disconnected: Introduced as workaround to enable OT in masked flows, but doubles vocabulary (50,257→100,514)—substantial cost inadequately discussed. Performance gains not clearly attributed to OT vs. multimask design itself.
Limited novelty of multimask approach: Using multiple mask tokens is straightforward; doesn't represent a significant conceptual advance.
Scattered presentation: Paper attempts to cover OT theory + two bound variants + multimask flows without clear unifying narrative. Relationship between contributions unclear.

Restricted applicability of main theorem: Results apply only to per-position flows with convex interpolants. While claimed to cover 'usual' flows, this is a meaningful restriction deserving deeper analysis.
Insufficient ablations: No systematic study of similarity measure choices, when OT helps vs. hurts, or comparison with other recent discrete flow methods beyond SEDD.
Missing scalability analysis: All experiments at GPT-2 scale; no evaluation on larger models. OT overhead analysis assumes fixed sequence length; behavior with variable lengths unclear.

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical framework: Theorem 3.1 establishes a categorical Benamou-Brenier-type theorem for DFM that is rigorously derived and connects dynamic and Kantorovich formulations with natural cost functions (Hamming, L2)
Principled perplexity bounds for DFM: Theorems 4.1-4.2 provide computable upper bounds enabling model evaluation and comparison across frameworks, with 0.96 correlation to generative perplexity
Practical efficiency gains: Minibatch OT achieves 8-fold inference reduction (1024→128 steps) with only ~3.4% training overhead, favorable scaling analysis demonstrates applicability
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple scales (Shakespeare to GPT-2/OWT), extensive ablations (OT solver, batch size, embedding dimension), proper entropy and diversity analysis
Sound technical execution: Proofs appear correct, experimental methodology is rigorous, broad empirical evaluation across metrics and datasets
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Minibatch OT from Tong et al. (2024), bounds inspired by Lou et al. (2024) and Haxholli et al. (2025), concurrent Shaul et al. (2025) achieves similar results—contribution is primarily application rather than fundamental innovation

Bounds are loose and impractical: ~11% gap above ground truth even in simplified settings (Section C.5); require intractable probability ratios (Eq. 140-141) to compute; heuristic approximation needed for OT-trained models, undermining 'principled evaluation' claims

Modest empirical improvements: OT contribution alone is 1-4% at many inference steps (Table 3); DFM-MMLM gains mostly from multimask, not OT; still substantially worse than GPT-2 (77.87 vs 58.92 on LM1B)
Restricted theoretical scope: Theorem 3.1 applies only to convex interpolant flows; while standard, claim of 'all usual flows' overstates generality; Remark 3.4 defense feels post-hoc

Multimask design concerns: Doubles vocabulary (50,257→100,514) with unquantified memory/computational overhead; equal mass distribution on 50,257^L is arbitrary; missing ablations on source distribution choice and design rationale
